headline: Microsoft explodes +15% on blockbuster earnings — the biggest mover in your portfolio tonight — while US-Iran strikes dominate world news and the ASX closed flat.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft reported a massive earnings beat last night — Azure cloud revenue grew 43% year-on-year, smashing analyst estimates. The market loved it, sending the stock up over 15% in one session. This is AI spending paying off in real numbers, and it dragged the broader NASDAQ up with it.

movers.name: Global X Artificial Intelligence ETF
movers.note: GXAI surged today on the ASX, riding the coattails of Microsoft's monster earnings result overnight. Microsoft is one of the biggest AI plays in the ETF, so a 15%+ jump in MSFT lifts the whole basket. Still down ~17% overall from your cost base, but this is a meaningful recovery session.

movers.name: Vanguard FTSE Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: Emerging markets ETF had a solid session today, up 2.1%. The Aussie dollar also rose strongly (now 70.4 US cents), which can push AUD-hedged or unhedged EM holdings. Broader global risk appetite improved off the back of the strong US tech earnings.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market Shares ETF
movers.note: VTS edged up today on the ASX, reflecting the strong NASDAQ and S&P 500 performance from last night's session. Microsoft's earnings were a tide that lifted most boats across US equities.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG ticked up today — a broad diversified ETF like this benefits from risk-on sentiment globally. Nothing specific driving it beyond the positive macro backdrop from strong US tech results.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Take-Two nudged up slightly last night. No major news catalysts — GTA 6 speculation continues to swirl online (a 'Trailer 3 tease' has fans excited), but nothing confirmed. The stock is just drifting along with the broader market lift.

movers.name: Alphabet Inc. (Google)
movers.note: Google dipped slightly last night, down 0.6%. The stock is still digesting its own recent earnings, where results were solid but the market reaction was muted. Analysts at Morningstar are debating whether it's fairly valued at current levels (~17.7x earnings). Microsoft's AI narrative is currently stealing the spotlight.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: PLS slipped 1.4% today despite reporting 31% growth in lithium volumes for the June 2026 quarter. The problem is the lithium price remains weak, so more volume doesn't automatically mean more profit. The market is still cautious on the lithium sector generally — your position is down 38% from cost.

watch_today.title: MSFT: Monster earnings — hold and enjoy the ride
watch_today.detail: Microsoft surged 15.5% last night after reporting Azure cloud revenue grew 43% year-on-year, well above the ~$38.2B analyst estimate (actual: $39.3B). Your MSFT position is now up ~1.8% overall. For a long-term holder, this is exactly why you stay in — the AI investment thesis is playing out in real earnings. No reason to sell. Hold confidently.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX: Big bounce today — still underwater, but the thesis is intact
watch_today.detail: GXAI jumped 6.36% today on the ASX, directly driven by Microsoft's blowout results. The ETF holds major AI names and when MSFT rips, GXAI follows. You're still down ~17% on this position overall, but the AI capex story is strengthening — Microsoft, Google and others are all spending heavily. Long-term hold.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX: Weak session despite good production numbers — long-term patience required
watch_today.detail: Pilbara Minerals dropped 1.4% today even after reporting 31% volume growth in the June quarter. The problem is weak lithium prices mean more lithium sold doesn't translate to better profits right now. At -38% on your cost base, this is painful — but the structural case for lithium in the energy transition is intact. Only consider selling if you no longer believe in that long-term story. Otherwise, sit tight.

watch_today.title: Middle East conflict escalating — watch oil prices
watch_today.detail: The US struck dozens of targets in Iran overnight, and Iran retaliated by targeting US bases in Kuwait. Oil (WTI) actually dipped 1.4% to $82.45 last night — markets are pricing in supply disruption risk but haven't panicked yet. If the conflict escalates further this weekend, expect oil to spike Monday, which would push inflation higher globally. Worth watching closely.

watch_today.title: AUD/USD surging — headwind for your US holdings in AUD terms
watch_today.detail: The Aussie dollar jumped 1.1% to 70.4 US cents last night — its highest in a while. This is good news generally (stronger economy signal), but it does mean your US-denominated holdings (MSFT, GOOG, TTWO) are worth slightly less when converted back to AUD. Not a reason to do anything — just good context for your portfolio.

watch_today.title: RBA rate outlook shifting — good news for your ASX holdings
watch_today.detail: The RBA admitted inflation is 'softer than we thought' this week, and markets are now pricing in a lower chance of further rate hikes. Lower rates are generally positive for shares, especially growth-oriented ETFs like VDHG and GXAI. Some economists still warn rates could rise, so this isn't a done deal — but the direction of travel looks more favourable.

world.summary: The biggest story in the world right now is the US military striking Iran, with Iran firing back at US bases in the region — the Middle East is on the brink of a wider war. Elsewhere, US election integrity concerns are growing, and European carmakers are struggling against Chinese competition.

stories.title: US strikes 'dozens of targets' in Iran — Middle East on the brink of regional war
stories.why_it_matters: The US launched strikes on dozens of Iranian targets overnight, with Saudi Arabia also reportedly involved. Iraq says it had no prior knowledge of the attacks and was blindsided. Iran responded by firing on US military bases in Kuwait. Trump has also claimed a Gaza ceasefire deal has been reached, though details are unconfirmed. This is the most significant direct US-Iran military confrontation in years — if it escalates, oil prices, global markets, and regional stability are all at serious risk.

stories.title: Iran retaliates — targets US bases in Kuwait as conflict widens
stories.why_it_matters: Following US strikes on Iranian soil, Iran fired back at US military installations in Kuwait. This marks a dangerous expansion of the conflict beyond Iranian borders. Iraq, caught in the middle geographically, says it was given no warning. Analysts are warning the strikes risk pulling more countries into the conflict and could destabilise the entire region. For everyday Australians, this means potential fuel price rises and global economic uncertainty if it escalates further.

stories.title: Iran fighting on multiple fronts as internal crises mount
stories.why_it_matters: Iran is not just dealing with US military pressure — the country is reportedly facing mounting internal economic and political crises simultaneously. A government under pressure from multiple directions is less predictable, which makes miscalculation more likely. This background context matters for understanding why the current escalation is particularly dangerous — Iran may feel it has less to lose.

stories.title: Trump's election interference claims undermined by declassified intelligence
stories.why_it_matters: The Trump administration's claims that foreign powers interfered in US elections are being called into doubt after newly declassified intelligence was released. Separately, the White House has levelled a new allegation that China swept up US voter data. With US midterm elections on the horizon, Trump is also attacking mail-in voting and raising concerns about the Postal Service. This is creating a volatile political environment in the US that could affect market sentiment and the lead-up to elections.

stories.title: European car giants struggling against Chinese competition and tariff uncertainty
stories.why_it_matters: European car manufacturers — think BMW, Mercedes, Volkswagen — are being squeezed from multiple directions: cheap Chinese EVs undercutting them on price, ongoing tariff uncertainty from the US, and a shaky global economy. This is a slow-moving structural crisis for one of Europe's most important industries. For Australian investors, it's a reminder of the global trade tensions that can ripple through diversified ETFs holding international shares.

markets.summary: Last night's US session was a cracker — NASDAQ surged 2.78% and the S&P 500 gained 1.66%, almost entirely driven by Microsoft's blockbuster earnings result. The ASX had a much quieter day, essentially flat (+0.1%). Gold hit $4,130 USD as investors also sought safety amid the Iran conflict, and the Aussie dollar pushed up to 70.4 cents.

indicators.name: ASX 200
indicators.note: Flat session on the ASX today — the big US tech moves hadn't fully flowed through yet.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Strong last night, led by Microsoft's earnings beat and broad tech optimism.

indicators.name: NASDAQ Composite
indicators.note: Best night in a while for the NASDAQ — Microsoft's 15% surge dragged the whole index up.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Oil actually fell despite US-Iran strikes — markets aren't panicking on supply yet, but watch this space.

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Gold nudging higher as geopolitical tension pushes investors toward safe havens.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: Aussie dollar up strongly to 70.4 US cents — a headwind for your US holdings when converted to AUD.

politics.summary: The RBA's inflation admission is reshaping interest rate expectations, while the Opposition attacks Albanese on Indigenous affairs and analysts debate whether rate hikes are truly off the table.

stories.title: RBA admits inflation is 'softer than we thought' — rate hike odds fall
stories.why_it_matters: The Reserve Bank of Australia has publicly acknowledged that inflation is coming in softer than expected. This is significant because it reduces the likelihood of further interest rate hikes, which is good news for mortgage holders and for the sharemarket. Traders and economists are now pricing in a lower chance of a rate rise at upcoming RBA meetings. If the RBA holds or cuts, that's a tailwind for growth assets like your ETFs.

stories.title: Economists warn: don't get too comfortable — rate rises still possible
stories.why_it_matters: Not everyone is convinced the RBA is done raising rates. Several economists quoted by the AFR are warning that while inflation looks soft now, underlying price pressures in services and wages haven't fully resolved. They suggest the RBA may be forced to hike again later in 2026 if the labour market stays tight. It's a timely reminder that the 'rates are done' narrative isn't universal.

stories.title: Opposition's Leeser accuses Albanese of losing direction on Indigenous affairs
stories.why_it_matters: Opposition spokesperson Julian Leeser has publicly accused Prime Minister Albanese of losing his way on Indigenous policy, following the failed Voice referendum. This signals the Coalition intends to keep pressure on Labor over Indigenous affairs as a political wedge. No immediate policy implications for investors, but it reflects an ongoing political vulnerability for the Albanese government.

stories.title: ASX small caps tipped for a breakout — investors watching closely
stories.why_it_matters: Some investors are tipping that ASX small-cap stocks — which have been beaten up for the past couple of years — could be about to outperform. The logic is that a softer inflation outlook and potential rate cuts would disproportionately benefit smaller companies that rely more on borrowed money. This is more of a broad market theme than something directly relevant to your current holdings, but worth knowing as context.

ai.summary: The big AI story this week is that the companies building AI — OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta — are asking governments to slow down one particular type of AI development: systems that can write and improve their own code. Meanwhile, Microsoft's earnings prove AI is now generating real commercial returns.

stories.title: OpenAI and Anthropic ask US government to slow down 'self-improving' AI
stories.why_it_matters: OpenAI and Anthropic — two of the biggest AI labs in the world — have formally asked the US government to consider placing restrictions on AI systems that can write and improve their own code (sometimes called 'recursive self-improvement'). This is notable because it's the companies building the technology asking for guardrails on their own products. Over 1,100 employees from OpenAI, Meta, Google and Anthropic signed a letter backing global safeguards. The concern is that AI that rewrites itself could improve faster than humans can monitor or control it.

stories.title: Microsoft's Azure AI revenue up 43% — proof that AI spending is working
stories.why_it_matters: Microsoft's Q4 results showed its cloud and AI division (Azure) grew revenue 43% year-on-year, beating analyst expectations of $38.2B with an actual $39.3B. This is a milestone moment — it shows that the billions being poured into AI infrastructure are starting to come back as real revenue. The stock jumped over 15% in one session. For anyone holding AI-related investments (like GXAI.AX), this is a very positive signal that the commercial case for AI is real, not just hype.

stories.title: India's Sarvam builds 1 trillion parameter AI model to challenge OpenAI and Anthropic
stories.why_it_matters: Indian AI startup Sarvam has announced it is building a one-trillion parameter AI model — that's roughly the scale of the largest models from OpenAI and Google. They've also launched their Vision Edge product commercially. This shows the AI race is genuinely global, with well-funded challengers emerging from outside the US tech giants. More competition in AI is generally good for consumers and businesses that use AI tools.

stories.title: Ireland establishes dedicated AI regulator under new AI Regulation Bill 2026
stories.source: Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment
stories.why_it_matters: Ireland has formally set up a dedicated AI regulatory office under its new AI Regulation Bill 2026, appointing Paul Byrne as its first CEO. Ireland matters disproportionately in tech regulation because it's the European headquarters for most major US tech companies (Google, Meta, Microsoft, Apple). How Ireland interprets and enforces EU AI rules will directly affect how those companies operate across Europe — and potentially globally.

sport.summary: The Roosters put on a historic demolition of the Cowboys in Round 22, the Titans are signing players, and the Cats moved into the AFL top six with a gritty win over Collingwood.

stories.title: Roosters thrash Cowboys 82-12 — most points scored in NRL since 1935
stories.why_it_matters: The Sydney Roosters put 82 points on the North Queensland Cowboys last night at Queensland Country Bank Stadium — the highest score in an NRL game since 1935, more than 90 years ago. The Cowboys managed just 12 in reply. It was a complete humiliation, with one Roosters player achieving something not seen in 91 years of the game. The Cowboys will need a serious response when they return to Brisbane.

stories.title: Gold Coast Titans snap up two Panthers players in signing spree
stories.why_it_matters: The Gold Coast Titans are on a recruitment drive, reportedly signing two players from the Penrith Panthers. Cbus Super Stadium hosts the Titans vs Warriors clash this Saturday in Round 22. The Titans' recruitment activity suggests they're building for the future, even as this season's finals spot remains uncertain.

stories.title: Raiders dealt blow ahead of Round 22; Dragons make shock spine selection
stories.why_it_matters: The Canberra Raiders have been dealt a significant injury/availability blow ahead of their Round 22 clash against the Panthers at Glen Willow Oval on Saturday, with coach Ricky Stuart hinting at a secret 'x-factor' to compensate. The St George Illawarra Dragons have also made a surprise change to their spine (the key playmaking positions — halfback, five-eighth, hooker) ahead of tonight's game against the Dolphins at WIN Stadium.

stories.title: Geelong Cats claw into AFL top six with win over Collingwood
stories.why_it_matters: Geelong won a topsy-turvy AFL match against Collingwood (the Pies), using a first-half blitz to set up the victory. The win lifts the Cats into the top six on the AFL ladder — an important milestone with finals positioning heating up. Carlton's big forward (nicknamed 'Big H') has also returned for a blockbuster upcoming clash, according to the club's team news.
